items.question: Which of these is an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
items.explanation: Abiotic components are non-living physical factors such as temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals.

items.question: Which of these is a natural ecosystem?
items.explanation: Ponds, lakes and forests form naturally; gardens, crop-fields and aquaria are set up by people.

items.question: Why is a garden considered an ecosystem?
options: Its organisms interact with each other and are affected by its non-living components
items.explanation: Plants and animals in a garden interact, and their growth and activities depend on abiotic factors.

items.question: By which process do producers make their food?
items.explanation: Green plants and some bacteria use sunlight to make food by photosynthesis.

items.question: In a balanced aquarium, which organisms play the role of the producers?
items.explanation: Aquatic plants photosynthesise, providing food (and oxygen) for the animals in the tank.

items.question: What do producers do with the Sun's energy?
options: Reflect all of it back into space
Fix it as food energy and make it available to consumers
items.explanation: Producers capture solar energy and store it in food that heterotrophs then eat.

items.question: An organism lives in or on another living organism and feeds on it. Which type of consumer is it?
items.explanation: Parasites are one of the four groups of consumers, alongside herbivores, carnivores and omnivores.

items.question: What are organisms that eat both plants and animals called?
items.explanation: Omnivores feed on both plant and animal food.

items.question: Why do consumers depend on producers?
options: Producers shield them from UV radiation
They cannot make their own food and get it from producers directly or indirectly
items.explanation: All the food consumers eat starts with producers, even when it passes through other consumers first.

items.question: If there were no decomposers, what would happen to garbage and to dead plants and animals?
options: They would pile up and the soil would not be replenished
items.explanation: Without decomposers dead matter would not be broken down, and its nutrients would not return to the soil.

items.question: What happens to the simple inorganic substances released by decomposers?
options: They rise to the ozone layer
They go into the soil and are used again by plants
items.explanation: Decomposers recycle nutrients: plants take up what they release into the soil.

items.question: Which change describes what decomposers do to the substances in dead remains?
items.explanation: They break large organic molecules down into simple inorganic ones; producers do the reverse.

items.question: What is each step or level of a food chain called?
items.explanation: Each feeding step in a food chain is a trophic level.

items.question: Which trophic level usually has the greatest number of individuals?
options: The producers at the first level
items.explanation: Lower levels generally hold more individuals, and the producers are the most numerous.

items.question: Small carnivores that feed on herbivores belong to which group?
options: Producers at the first trophic level
Primary consumers at the second trophic level
Secondary consumers at the third trophic level
items.explanation: Herbivores are primary consumers; animals that eat them are secondary consumers on the third level.

items.question: When primary consumers eat green plants, where does a great deal of the energy in the food go?
options: It is lost as heat to the environment
It goes back to the Sun
It is stored in the ozone layer
All of it becomes body mass
items.explanation: Much of the energy escapes as heat, and some is used in digestion and work, leaving only a little for growth.

items.question: Why do food chains generally have only three or four steps?
options: So much energy is lost at each step that little usable energy is left after four levels
Decomposers end every chain after three steps
Animals cannot eat more than four kinds of food
items.explanation: With only about 10% passed on each time, the energy left after four levels is too small to support another.

items.question: The flow of energy in an ecosystem is unidirectional. What does this mean?
options: Energy cycles back to the Sun
Energy moves only from consumers to producers
Energy moves forward through the trophic levels and does not return to earlier ones
New energy is created at each level
items.explanation: Energy captured by plants passes on to herbivores and beyond but never flows back to the earlier level.

items.question: What is a food web made up of?
items.explanation: A food web is a network formed by many food chains that share organisms.

items.question: Which statement about the length and complexity of food chains is correct?
options: They always have exactly three steps
They are identical in every ecosystem
items.explanation: Food chains differ widely from one ecosystem to another, and they branch into food webs.

items.question: In a food web, one kind of prey disappears. What will most likely happen to a predator that feeds on several kinds of prey?
options: It survives by feeding more on its other prey
items.explanation: Because organisms in a web have several food sources, losing one does not necessarily starve the predator.

items.question: How do pesticides sprayed on crops get into the food chain?
options: They fall from the ozone layer
They are washed into soil and water and taken up by plants
Animals make them in their bodies
items.explanation: Plants absorb the chemicals with water and minerals from the soil, and aquatic plants take them up from water.

items.question: Why do food grains, vegetables and even meat contain pesticide residues?
options: Pesticides used on crops enter food chains and accumulate in them
items.explanation: Pesticides from farming reach our food through the food chain and are stored along the way.

items.question: Can pesticide residues in food always be removed by washing?
options: No, washing and other methods do not always get rid of them
Yes, washing removes all of them
Yes, boiling destroys all of them
items.explanation: Residues are inside the food itself, so washing does not always get rid of them.

items.question: Which harmful effect of UV radiation on humans does the chapter mention?
items.explanation: UV radiation damages organisms; in humans it is known to cause skin cancer.

items.question: What did the agreement forged by UNEP in 1987 do?
items.explanation: The UN Environment Programme agreement capped CFC production; CFC-free refrigerators are now mandatory.

items.question: Ozone is a deadly poison, yet the ozone layer is essential. Why?
options: It provides the oxygen we breathe
It traps heat that plants need
High in the atmosphere it shields the Earth from UV radiation
items.explanation: Ozone would be harmful to breathe, but at high altitude it blocks damaging UV radiation.

items.question: Which item of household waste would be broken down by microorganisms in the soil?
items.explanation: Tea leaves are biodegradable; plastic and glass are not broken down by biological processes.

items.question: What can non-biodegradable substances do in the environment?
options: Always disappear within a few days
Persist for a long time or harm members of the ecosystem
items.explanation: Such substances may be inert and simply remain, or they may harm living things in the ecosystem.

items.question: Clay cups (kulhads) were suggested to replace plastic cups on trains. What problem would making them on a large scale cause?
items.explanation: Clay for millions of cups would come from the top-soil, so a 'natural' alternative can still harm the environment.

items.question: What has caused much of our waste to become non-biodegradable?
items.explanation: New kinds of packaging, and the habit of using disposable things, add non-biodegradable waste.
